summary: One of the periodic IAB status reports on which Internet protocols were at which stage of standardization. It was issued quarterly. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1200.

eli5.summary: A school chart saying which lessons are done. This is the edition from 1990, updated four times a year.

subtitle: Updated listing of Internet protocol standardization status

tldr.problem: The Internet's protocol landscape was evolving rapidly in 1990, with new protocols proposed regularly and old ones either advancing or becoming obsolete.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB issued RFC 1140 as the May 1990 snapshot of protocol status, published quarterly. It categorized protocols into five states (standard, draft standard, proposed, experimental, historic) and four requirement levels (required, recommended, elective, limited use, not recommended).
tldr.outcome: This quarterly memo became the definitive reference for protocol status. It was more detailed than its predecessor and was later superseded by RFC 1200.

today: RFC 1140 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 1200 as the next quarterly update to the protocol standards status.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1140 is the May 1990 edition of the IAB's official protocol standards status report. Issued quarterly, it describes the state of standardization of all known Internet protocols and provides context about the standardization process, the RFC series, and the role of related reference documents.

The memo emphasizes that copies should be no more than three months old. It directs readers to section 6.1 for a summary of recent changes, which tracks new RFCs and protocols that have changed status since the previous edition.
sections.eli5: This is the 1990 version of the protocol status list. The Internet Activities Board updates it four times a year to keep everyone current.

sections.title: Protocol States and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
Every Internet protocol is classified along two independent dimensions. The protocol state (or maturity level) describes where the protocol is in its life cycle: standard (approved by the IAB), draft standard (actively being considered), proposed standard (may be considered for standardization), experimental (research-focused, not for operational use), or historic (obsolete or unused).

The requirement level (or status) indicates how widely it should be deployed: required (all systems must implement it), recommended (systems should implement it), elective (optional based on system functionality), limited use (for specific purposes only), or not recommended (discouraged due to experimental or historic status).

RFC 1140 adds a refinement compared to RFC 1100: it introduces the limited use category for protocols that have a specific, restricted purpose. It also provides a detailed decision table and a visual diagram showing how protocols move along the standards track from proposed through draft to standard status.
sections.eli5: Each protocol gets two grades: whether it's done (standard), being tested (proposed), or retired (historic), and whether everyone must use it (required) or it's optional (elective).

sections.title: The Standards Track Path
sections.content:
RFC 1140 clarifies the progression of protocols through the standards track. A new protocol starts as proposed standard, marked for future consideration by the IAB. During this phase, implementation and testing by several groups is desirable, and revisions are likely.

A proposed standard with implementation experience and a sponsor (someone to represent it to the IAB) can advance to draft standard status. A draft standard undergoes review by the entire Internet community for a minimum of six months. This state serves as a warning that unless objections are raised or flaws are found, the protocol will become an official standard.

After sufficient time and without serious objections, the IAB may declare a draft standard to be an official standard. Once designated as standard, a protocol has the full backing of the IAB and is considered mature for deployment.

Protocols that become obsolete or superseded by better alternatives are declared historic. Experimental protocols are separate from the standards track and are not intended for general operational use.
sections.eli5: Protocols start as proposals, get tested and reviewed, then become official standards. Old ones are marked historic. This memo shows which stage each protocol is at.

sections.title: Supporting Reference Documents
sections.content:
RFC 1140 references several companion documents that provide more detail. Assigned Numbers lists the numeric identifiers used throughout Internet protocols, such as protocol numbers and port assignments. Annotated Internet Protocols (superseding the previous Official Protocols document) describes each protocol and notes any known problems or ongoing experiments.

Gateway Requirements and Host Requirements clarify the specifications that apply to routers and host systems respectively, resolving ambiguities in the core protocol specifications. These requirements documents help implementers understand exactly which protocols must be implemented on which types of systems.

The MIL-STD specifications for IP, TCP, FTP, SMTP, and Telnet are also mentioned as authoritative parallel documents that implementers should consult.
sections.eli5: Other documents list protocol numbers, explain what routers and computers must do, and describe any problems with the protocols.

sections.title: Organization and Updates
sections.content:
RFC 1140 organizes protocols into sections based on their standardization state: standard protocols, network-specific standard protocols, draft standard protocols, proposed standard protocols, experimental protocols, and historic protocols. Each section lists the protocol name, requirement level, and the RFC number(s) defining it.

Section 6.1 is particularly important for readers tracking changes: it lists recent changes including new RFCs, protocols that have changed category or status, and technical updates to existing protocols. This allows readers to quickly identify what has changed since the previous quarterly edition.

The memo emphasizes that implementers should verify they have the most recent RFC for each protocol of interest, and that RFC 1140 itself is the authoritative reference for determining which RFC describes the current specification.
sections.eli5: The memo lists protocols in groups by their status. A special section tracks what changed since the last edition, so you can see what's new without reading the whole thing.
